description_full: Performance Food Group Company, through its subsidiaries, markets and distributes food and food-related products in North America. It operates through three segments: Foodservice, Convenience, and Specialty. The company offers beef, pork, poultry, seafood, frozen food, refrigerated products, and dry groceries to disposables, cleaning and kitchen supplies, and related products, as well as value-added services, such as product selection and procurement, menu development, and operational strategies to independent restaurants, chain restaurants, and other institutional food-away-from-home locations. It also provides wholesale consumer products, including cigarettes and alternative nicotine products, candy, snacks, fresh products, groceries, dairy, bread, beverages, general merchandise, and health and beauty care products to traditional convenience stores, drug stores, mass merchants, grocery stores, liquor stores, and other specialty and small format stores. In addition, the company distributes candy, snacks, beverages, fresh and frozen perishable food, and other non-food items. Performance Food Group Company was founded in 1885 and is headquartered in Richmond, Virginia.

financial_summary: Performance Food Group Company is a large-cap consumer defensive business with a $17.0B market cap on $67.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +6% over the past three years and +15% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.

Returns on capital run at 7% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 12% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $1.0B in free cash flow — roughly 2 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 3.93× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.9× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and thin 2.1× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Shareholder yield is only 0.0%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 4.2% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.2× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 1% operating margin trails the Consumer Defensive median (7%) by 6pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.16x its revenue share).
It accounts for 2.0% of sector revenue and 0.3% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+31.0% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.07 across 172 companies in the universe; the top four hold 38% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 8% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 33% and a beta of 0.94, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.35 vs 5y 0.93), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $132.2M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 79% in the 2020 crash and 32% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades only 11% below its DCF fair value of $121, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 71%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $78.78 to $182 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Defensive peers: P/E 42.8 vs 18.5 and EV/EBITDA 14.3 vs 10.3 (sector median).
The EBIT multiple is close to its own 10-year median (-3%).
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 6.1% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The 12 covering analysts target $124 on average, 15% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 7% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.6%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.55).
It runs a 12% gross margin and converts 2% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 3.93x.
ROE of 7% is amplified by 3.8x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.9x net debt to EBITDA ($35.9M of cash against $5.0B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, and interest cover is thin at 2.1x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 4.8, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 5.8% over 3 years, 17.4% over 5 years and 15.5% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 18%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Capex runs only 0.5x depreciation (0.6% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 19, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
Analysts expect 19.0% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own a modest 4.2%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (10 sales, net $2.2M sold).
The share count has grown 0.5% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
people: With about 44,000 employees, each generates about $1.5M of revenue, 3.0x the Consumer Defensive median, and productivity has risen 15.5% a year.
That works out to $23K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.9M (2x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
